The oldest classical source of Chinese medicine is the Huangdi Neijing ("Yellow Emperor's Inner Canon"), a collection of texts assembled in layers between the Warring States period and the Han dynasty (approximately the 4th–1st centuries BCE; the exact dating is disputed). The current form of the Suwen is based on a commented edition from the 8th century (Wang Bing). It has two main sections, the Suwen ("Basic Questions") and the Lingshu ("Spiritual Pivot"), presented as dialogues between the emperor and his physicians. The Lingshu describes needles, meridians and needling techniques. The text is not the work of a single author, and its attribution to a mythical emperor is a literary convention.

From China, the practice traveled east. Via Buddhist and diplomatic routes it reached Korea and Japan in the first centuries CE (in Japan, mainly from the 6th century), and there it acquired its own forms, for example the Japanese style, gentler, with very thin needles. In Europe, information arrived through Jesuit missionaries in the 17th century, and the Dutch physician Willem ten Rhijne wrote about acupuncture in 1683. In the 20th century, the French diplomat Georges Soulié de Morant popularized it in France. Western interest grew greatly after 1971–1972, when the American president's visit to China and a press report about a surgical operation drew public attention.

Chronic pain: the review by Vickers et al. (2018) found a modest effect versus sham and a larger one versus no treatment. The guidelines contradict each other: the American College of Physicians (2017) includes acupuncture among the non-pharmacological options for low back pain, based on low to moderate quality evidence, while the NICE NG59 guideline (2016) recommended that acupuncture not be offered for low back pain. EAV (Voll electroacupuncture) and bioresonance claim to measure the skin's electrical conductance at points and to be able to detect allergies, infections or organ imbalances. Controlled studies have not shown that these measurements reliably distinguish people with and without allergies or other conditions; the device gives values that can be influenced by electrode pressure and skin moisture. These devices can lead to false diagnoses or unnecessary expense. Ryodoraku, a Japanese method of measuring conductance, raises similar questions about reliability.

The yin meridians of the hand (LU, PC, HT) run along the inner side of the arm; the yang ones of the hand (LI, TE, SI) along the outer side. The yin meridians of the foot (SP, LR, KI) run along the inner side of the lower limb; the yang ones (ST, GB, BL) along the outer, anterior, lateral or posterior side. Each yin meridian is paired with a yang one, as a related "pair": LU–LI, ST–SP, HT–SI, BL–KI, PC–TE, GB–LR. Moxibustion uses Artemisia (mugwort) leaves burned near the points. Traditionally, it is said to "warm the meridians" and expel "cold". Types: direct moxa (a small cone on the skin, which can leave a scar and is rarely practiced), indirect moxa (with a layer of ginger, garlic or salt between the cone and the skin), the moxa stick held above the skin, and box moxa. The main risk is burns, followed by smoke, which can irritate the airways; the space must be ventilated. It is avoided in case of fever, on damaged skin, on the face, in pregnancy (abdominal area) and in people with reduced sensitivity. Evidence: there are studies for some situations, such as turning a fetus from breech presentation, but the quality is low or variable, and the practice is done only under obstetric supervision, not at home.
